This is a fresh, independent resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi*, a new sentence beginning a separate thought), because what precedes it serves as an introduction to it, preparing the listener to receive this admonition. The terror and warning that came before it prepare the soul to accept the admonition, for an admonition sinks deeper into the heart at such a time, because the listener feels his soul humbled and his heart softened. Thus the tyranny of stubbornness and obstinacy departs from him, and in souls there arises an expectation of something to follow.

The vocative (*nidaʾ*) is for alerting, an alert that signals the importance of what is said and calls the listener to hear it. The vocative is not used in its literal sense, since it does not intend to request attention, nor is it directed at a specific individual or a specific group. Rather, the speaker makes it addressed to everyone who hears it, intentionally or unintentionally.

The definite article in *al-insān* (the human being) is the definite article of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), and this is how the majority of the exegetes (*jumhūr al-mufassirīn*) understood it. That is, the intended meaning is not a particular human being. The indication of this is the context of the speech, together with His words that follow it: ﴿Nay, you deny the Judgment. And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ (al-Infitar: 9) and the verse after it.

This general address is intended to refer to those who denied resurrection, as indicated by its occurring immediately after the warning of the coming of resurrection, and His words after it, ﴿Nay, you deny the Judgment﴾ (al-Infitar: 9), confirm this. The meaning is: O human being who denied resurrection. None who denies resurrection would be anything but a polytheist, because denial of resurrection and polytheism are mutually entailing at that time. So this is a general term intended in a specific sense by means of the context, or it is a customary generalization (*istighrāq ʿurfī*), since the majority of those addressed when the Islamic call first appeared were polytheists.

As for what is in His words ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord﴾, the interrogative (*mā*) asks about the thing that deceived the polytheist, leading him to associate partners with his Lord and to deny resurrection.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAṭāʾ that the human being here is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra. It is reported from ʿIkrima that the intended one is Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the intended one is Abū al-Ashadd ibn Kalada al-Jumaḥī. And it is reported from al-Kalbī and Muqātil that it was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn Sharīq.

The interrogative is a figurative use (*majāz*) expressing denial and wonder at associating partners with Allah. That is: there is no cause for polytheism and denial of resurrection except that this is a deception that deceived him away from us. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for the fact that polytheism does not occur to a sane person's mind except that someone deceives him into it. Thus it is possible that deception exists, and it is possible that there is no deception.

Deception (*ghurūr*) is enticing someone with what the deceived one imagines to be benefit while it is harm. Its verb may be attributed to the entity of the one who entices, literally, as in ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾, or figuratively, as in ﴿and the worldly life has deceived you﴾ (al-Jathiya: 35), since life is the time of deception. It may also be attributed literally to an abstract meaning, as in ﴿Let not the going about of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 196), and in the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*Has your love for me, which will kill me, deceived you?*

Or figuratively, as in His words, ﴿decorated speech as deception﴾ (al-Anʿām: 112).

Its verb takes one direct object. Sometimes, together with its object, the name of that concerning whose affairs the deception occurs is mentioned, and it is then transitive through the preposition *bi* (with/concerning). The meaning of *bi* here is accompaniment (*mulābasa*), as in His words: ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾. That is: let not a deception that is clothed in the affairs of Allah deceive you, that is, accompanying the affairs of Allah in a figurative accompaniment. It is not the *bi* of causality, as one says: he deceived him with giving up wealth, or he deceived him with speech. Since the nature of accompaniment cannot be conceived with entities themselves, when *bi* of accompaniment enters upon the name of an entity, it is necessarily understood that there is an implied matter of the entity's affairs understood from the context. So the meaning here is: what deceived you into associating partners with your Lord, as His words indicate: ﴿Who created you, proportioned you, and balanced you﴾ (al-Infitar: 7), for the one who denies resurrection at that time would be none but a polytheist.

The choice of describing Allah as "your Lord" rather than mentioning the name of majesty (Allah) is because the meaning of "Lord" includes sovereignty, origination, and kindness. In it there is a reminder to the human being of what necessitates that the Lord deserves obedience from His creature. So it is an indirect rebuke.

Likewise, the use of the description "the Generous" rather than any other of Allah's attributes is to remind people of His blessing upon them and His kindness toward them, for the Generous is deserving of gratitude and obedience.

The third description, contained in the relative clause ﴿and balanced you, in whatever form He willed He assembled you﴾, comprises much of what the first two descriptions indicate, for creation, proportioning, balancing, and beautifying the form are all forms of kindness to the creature, and they are blessings upon him. All of this is an indirect rebuke for ungratefulness for His blessing by worshipping other than Him.

It is mentioned from Ṣāliḥ ibn Mismār that he said: "It has reached us that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said: 'His ignorance deceived him.'" He did not mention a chain of narration (*isnād*).

The enumeration of the relative clauses, although some of them may suffice in place of others, since proportioning is a state of creation and its mention may suffice in place of mentioning creation, as in His words ﴿and He proportioned them as seven heavens﴾ (al-Baqara: 29), nevertheless the intent is to make manifest the levels of blessing. This is elaboration (*itnāb*) intended to remind of each relative clause and to make a person stop and reflect on each one specifically. Among the requirements of elaboration is the context of rebuke.

Creation (*khalq*) is bringing into existence according to a intended measure.

Proportioning (*taswiya*) is making a thing *sawiyy*, that is, upright and sound. Among proportioning is making its powers and its inherent benefits balanced and not uneven in the effects of their performing their functions, such that when some of them are disturbed, disturbance reaches the rest, and a deficiency arises in perception or sensation, or a deviation of the temperament or a pain in it arises. Thus proportioning comprises this great meaning.

Balancing (*taʿdīl*) is harmony among the parts of the body, such as the harmony of the two hands, the two legs, the two eyes, and the form of the face, so that there is no disparity between their pairs, nor any ugliness in their totality. It also includes making him upright in stature, for if one of the hands were on the side and the other on the back, their function would be disrupted, and if the eyes were placed at the back, the benefit of sight while walking would be lost. Likewise the placement of the internal organs: the throat, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the two kidneys, and the place of the two lungs, the heart, the brain, and the spinal cord.

Allah created the human body with its organs and limbs divided into two sides, with no disparity between one side and the other, and placed on each side the like of what is on the other of veins, nerves, and arteries.

The verb *sawwāka* is connected by the particle *fāʾ* (then) to *khalaqaka*, and the verb *ʿaddalaka* is connected by *fāʾ* to *sawwāka*, in order (*tafrīʿan fī al-dhikr*), in view of their meanings being sequential in the reckoning of the one who considers, though all of them occur at one time, since they are stages of formation from the time he is a lump of flesh until the completion of his creation. So the *fāʾ* in their conjunction is in its best place, as in His words, ﴿Who created and proportioned, and Who determined and guided﴾ (al-Aʿlā: 2).

The majority read *fa-ʿaddalaka* with the *dāl* doubled (*tashdīd*). ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it with the *dāl* lightened. The two readings are close in meaning, except that the doubling indicates intensification in balance, that is, in proportioning, and so it conveys perfection of workmanship.

As for His words, ﴿in whatever form﴾: know that the original sense of *ayy* is that it is used for interrogation about distinguishing a thing from its counterparts in its condition, as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ (ʿAbasa: 18) in Surat ʿAbasa, and His words, ﴿then in what message after this will they believe?﴾.

Its use in interrogation often intends a metonymy for wonder or for making someone wonder at the status of that to which *ayy* is attached, because when a thing reaches a degree of perfection and greatness, strong enough that one asks about it and inquires about its state, from here arises the meaning of *ayy* indicating perfection. Its precise nature is that it is a metonymic meaning that has become frequent in their speech, and *ayy* here is truly the interrogative. This *ayy* in meaning functions as a qualifier of an indefinite noun, either as an adjective, as in: "He is a man, what a man!" or as a construct with an indefinite noun, as in this verse. So it is permissible for His words ﴿in whatever form﴾ to be connected with the verbs (*khalaqaka, sawwāka, ʿaddalaka*), in which case the pause is at ﴿in whatever form﴾.

It is also permissible for it to be connected with His words *rakkabaka* (He assembled you), in which case the pause is at His words *ʿaddalaka*, and His words *mā shāʾa* (what He willed) are a parenthetical insertion between ﴿in whatever form﴾ and *rakkabaka*.

The meaning on both readings: in a form of whatever form, that is, in a perfect, wondrous form.

The clause ﴿in whatever form He willed He assembled you﴾ explains the clause *ʿaddalaka*, given that the clause *ʿaddalaka* is derived from the clause *sawwāka*, which is derived from the clause *khalaqaka*, so its explanation is an explanation of both.

The *fī* (in) indicates the figurative sense of location, which is in the sense of accompaniment: He created you, proportioned you, and balanced you, accompanied by a wondrous form. So the position of ﴿in whatever form﴾ is the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the *kāf* of address, and the operator of the circumstance is *ʿaddalaka* or *rakkabaka*. The wondrous form is treated as a container for the thing formed with it, to indicate its being firmly established in what it describes.

*Mā* may be a relative pronoun whose referent is the assembling (*tarkīb*), and it is in the position of an absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*), and *shāʾa* is the relative clause of *mā*, and the returning pronoun is omitted, its estimate being *shāʾahu* (He willed it). The meaning: He assembled you with the assembling that He willed. Allah says: ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 6).

The explicit mention of the verbal noun of *rakkabaka* is avoided in favor of expressing it vaguely through the relative *mā*, to indicate the emphasis of the relative clause with what is in its clause of the will ascribed to the pronoun of the Lord, the Creator, the Originator, the Wise, and it is enough to suffice with it.

It is also permissible for the clause *shāʾa* to be an adjective of *ṣūra* (form), in which case the returning pronoun is omitted, and *mā* is an emphasizing addition. The estimate: in a great form that He willed with a particular willing, that is, by means of planning and determination.

In it there is a reminder to the human being of what necessitates that the Lord deserves obedience from His creature. So it is an indirect rebuke.

Likewise, the use of the description "the Generous" rather than any other of Allah's attributes is to remind people of His blessing upon them and His kindness toward them, for the Generous is deserving of gratitude and obedience.

It is mentioned from Ṣāliḥ ibn Mismār that he said: "It has reached us that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said: 'His ignorance deceived him.'" He did not mention a chain of narration (*isnād*).

This is elaboration (*itnāb*) intended to remind of each relative clause and to make a person stop and reflect on each one specifically. Among the requirements of elaboration is the context of rebuke.

Creation (*khalq*) is bringing into existence according to a intended measure.

Proportioning (*taswiya*) is making a thing *sawiyy*, that is, upright and sound. Among proportioning is making its powers and its inherent benefits balanced and not uneven in the effects of their performing their functions, such that when some of them are disturbed, disturbance reaches the rest, and a deficiency arises in perception or sensation, or a deviation of the temperament or a pain in it arises. Thus proportioning comprises this great meaning.

Balancing (*taʿdīl*) is harmony among the parts of the body, such as the harmony of the two hands, the two legs, the two eyes, and the form of the face, so that there is no disparity between their pairs, nor any ugliness in their totality. It also includes making him upright in stature, for if one of the hands were on the side and the other on the back, their function would be disrupted, and if the eyes were placed at the back, the benefit of sight while walking would be lost. Likewise the placement of the internal organs: the throat, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the two kidneys, and the place of the two lungs, the heart, the brain, and the spinal cord.

Allah created the human body with its organs and limbs divided into two sides, with no disparity between one side and the other, and placed on each side the like of what is on the other of veins, nerves, and arteries.

The verb *sawwāka* is connected by the particle *fāʾ* (then) to *khalaqaka*, and the verb *ʿaddalaka* is connected by *fāʾ* to *sawwāka*, in order (*tafrīʿan fī al-dhikr*), in view of their meanings being sequential in the reckoning of the one who considers, though all of them occur at one time, since they are stages of formation from the time he is a lump of flesh until the completion of his creation. ﴿Nay, but you deny the Recompense.﴾

*Kalla* (كَلّا, a particle of rebuke and refusal) is a deterrent from what is delusion regarding God, or from the delusion that comes from ﴿what has deceived you concerning your Lord﴾ [al-Infitar: 6]. This phrase includes the deceit that befalls a person through associating others with God, and his turning away from the blessings of God, the Exalted, through disbelief. Or it refers to the state of the polytheist being like the state of one who is deluded, as has been stated before in the two aspects of the denial implied by His words ﴿what has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord﴾ [al-Infitar: 6].

The meaning is: your associating others with your Creator is false, and it is a delusion, or like a delusion.

His words after it, ﴿but you deny the Recompense﴾, may be a *idrab intiqali* (إضراب انتقالي, a transitional "but" that turns to another subject) from the purpose of reproach and admonition for disbelief to the mention of another heinous crime, which is the denial of the Resurrection and the Recompense. The reproach and admonition include it, because *bal* (بَلْ) does not leave the sense of conjunction; that is, the conjunction is in the purpose, not in the attribution of the judgment. For this reason, the noun following it takes the same *i'rab* (إعراب, grammatical case-inflection) as the noun before it. The grammarians say that it is followed in its pronunciation but not in its judgment; that is, it is a following of relevance in the purpose, not a following in the attribution.

It is also possible that *kalla* is a negation of the existence of anything that would deceive a person into associating others with God; that is, there is no excuse for a person to associate others with God, since nothing exists that would deceive him into it.

His words ﴿but you deny﴾ would then be an *idrab ibtali* (إضراب إبطالي, a "but" of rejection), and what follows *bal* is an explanation of what emboldened them to associate others with God. This is not a delusion, since they have no doubt in associating others with God that would make the doubt like a delusion. Rather, they persisted in associating others with God because they confined themselves in a safe place from its consequences, so they chose to continue in it because it was the desire of their souls. They did not care that it is manifestly false. So they deny the Recompense. Therefore the firm resolve of all of them in doubt was the cause, despite the differences in their perceptions, of which the falsity of stones being gods is not hidden from some of them. Do you not see that they did not see any punishment except the punishment of this world?!

On this aspect, there is an indication that the denial of the Resurrection is the sum of the crimes. A parallel to this aspect occurs in His words, the Exalted: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe? And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate. Rather, those who disbelieve deny﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 20–22] in Surat al-Inshiqaq.

The majority (al-Jumhur, الجمهور) read ﴿تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ with the *ta'* of address (بتاء الخطاب). Abu Ja'far read it with the *ya'* of the third person (بياء الغيبة), by way of *iltifat* (الالتفات, a shift in grammatical person).

The present tense in His words ﴿you deny the Recompense﴾ indicates that their denial of the Recompense is continuous; they do not desist from it, and this is the cause of the continuation of their disbelief.

The present tense also brings the state of this denial into the present in a way that calls for wonder at their denial, because with them are the proofs which should have led their denial of the Recompense to cease.

*Al-Din* (الدين, the Religion/Recompense) here means the Recompense.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 82, verses 10–12:

﴿And indeed, over you are guardians,﴾ ﴿noble, recording,﴾ ﴿who know what you do.﴾

This is conjoined to the clause ﴿you deny the Din﴾ [al-Infitar: 9] as an emphasis on the certainty of recompense for deeds.

The statement is reinforced with the particle inna and the lam of initiation, because they deny this with strong denial.

The word ﴿guardians﴾ (la-hafizin) is an adjective of an omitted noun whose supposed form is: "la-malaikatun hafizin" (indeed, angels who are guardians), meaning: keeping count, not neglecting anything of your deeds.

The angels are mentioned in the plural in view of their distribution among people, since each person has two angels, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the two receivers receive, one on the right and one on the left, seated. He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer ready.﴾ [Qaf: 17]. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that each person has two angels who guard his deeds, and this, by its plain meaning, also indicates sufficiency regarding the occurrence of recompense, for if there were no recompense for deeds, the care in counting them would be pointless.

Four attributes are applied to the angels appointed to count people's deeds: guarding (al-hifz), nobility (al-karam), writing (al-kitabah), and knowledge of what people do (al-'ilm bima yaf'aluhu al-nas).

The first of these is mentioned, namely guarding, because it is the purpose for which the discourse preceded, which is the affirmation of recompense for all deeds. Then three further attributes are mentioned after it, by which the full extent of guarding and counting is achieved, and in them is an honouring of the status of the guardian angels.

As for guarding (al-hifz), it here means watching over and monitoring. In this sense it is transitive to its object by means of the preposition ʿalā, because it implies the meaning of monitoring. A ḥafīẓ is a watcher, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God is Watcher over them﴾ [al-Shura: 6].

This usage differs from the usage of hifz transitive to the object directly, where it means protection, as in His saying ﴿They guard him by the command of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11]. Thus hifz in this absolute sense combines the meaning of watchful care and the standing over what is entrusted to the guardian, and the trust regarding what is committed to him.

The preposition ʿalā here indicates elevation, because it implies the meaning of oversight and authority.

As for the attribute of nobility (karam), it is preciousness in kind, as was already discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said: O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29], in Surat al-Naml.

Nobility is therefore their inner quality, comprehensive of perfection in dealing and in the deeds that proceed from them. As for the attribute of writing, it is meant to signify the precise recording of what they were charged to preserve, a recording that is not subject to forgetting, nor to diminution, nor to addition. Thus "writing" is used metaphorically for this meaning, since the literal sense of writing as inscription is not possible in a manner suitable to the matters of the unseen.

As for the attribute of knowing what people do, it is the comprehension of what proceeds from people of deeds and of what occurs to their minds of thought intended for a good or evil act, which is intention (al-hamm).

Al-abrar is the plural of barr, with a fatha on the ba', which means the pious (al-taqi). It is an intensive form (fi'l) in the sense of the active participle (fa'il), derived from barra yabarru. Al-fujjar is the plural of fajir, and the pattern fu''al is regular for the broken plural of the sound-final-radical masculine active participle (fa'il).

We, the people of the Sunna, do not hold that eternal abiding in the Fire applies to anyone other than the disbeliever. As for the sinful believers, they will not abide eternally in the Fire, otherwise the benefit of faith would be nullified.

Al-na'im is the name of what a person enjoys.

The adverbial sense of His saying "fi na'im" (in bliss) is figurative, because bliss is a notional matter that cannot literally be a container; the continuity of their enjoyment is likened to the encompassing of the container around the contained, such that it never leaves them.

As for the adverbial sense of His saying ﴿la-fi jahim﴾ (indeed in the Blazing Fire), it is literal.

Al-jahim has become a proper name by predominance over Jahannam, and it has been discussed earlier in Surah al-Takwir and in Surah al-Nazi'at.

The clause (yaslawnaha) is either a descriptive clause for (jahim), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from al-fujjar, or a circumstantial clause from al-jahim. Sali al-nar means touching its heat to the body; it is said: salia al-nar, when one feels its heat, and its reality is the painful sensing of the fire's heat. When warming oneself is intended, it is said: istala.

The phrase yawm al-din is an adverbial complement of yaslawnaha, and it is mentioned to clarify that they burn in it as a recompense for their wickedness, because al-din is recompense, and yawm al-din is the day of recompense, which is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection.

{page 183}
The clause ﴿And they will never be absent from it﴾ is conjoined to the clause (yaslawnaha), meaning: they will burn with its heat and will not be separated from it, that is, they will abide eternally in it.

His saying ﴿wa-ma hum 'anha bi-ghaibin﴾ was given as a nominal sentence rather than saying "wa-ma yaghibuna 'anha" or "wa-ma yufariquunaha," in order to convey that the nominal sentence indicates permanence, whether in affirmation or negation; permanence is a state of the informative relation, whether it is a relation of affirmation or of negation, as in His saying: ﴿And they will not be brought out of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The addition of the ba' is for emphasizing the negation.

The fronting of (anha) before its complement is for concern with the prepositional phrase, and for keeping the rhyme (ri'ayah 'ala al-fasilah).

﴿Wa-mā adrāka mā yawmu al-dīn﴾ (And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?).

It may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah, a clause describing the state of the subject), and the wāw is the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl). It may also be a parenthetical clause (mu'tariḍah, inserted between other elements of speech) if ﴿yawma lā tamliku nafsun li-nafsin shay'an﴾ [Al-Infitar: 19] is taken as a substitute (badal) for yawma al-dīn, which is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyyah), as will come.

﴿Wa-mā adrāka mā yawmu al-dīn﴾ [Al-Infitar: 18] is a compound construction made of the interrogative mā and the verb of knowing (fi'l al-dirāyah), made transitive by the hamza (causative form), so that its subject becomes a third object in addition to the two objects of the verb darā. It belongs to the same pattern as a'lamu and arā. Thus the kāf is its first object, and it has been suspended (mu'allaq) with respect to the other two objects by the second interrogative mā.

The first interrogative is used figuratively (kināyatan) to express the magnitude and awesomeness of the Day, such that the speaker asks the listener about the thing that would make him know the reality of that Day. The intended meaning is that no knowledge of any knower can reach its true nature.

The second interrogative is literal: it is the question of one asking about the reality of the Day of Judgment, just as you say, "I know whether Zayd is standing," meaning "I know the answer to this question."

Such a construction, which has become like a proverb (jarā majrā al-mathal), is not changed in its wording. Its explanation has already been given in full at the Almighty's words ﴿Wa-mā adrāka mā al-ḥāqqah﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 3].

Verse 82:18: ﴿Then what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾

This is a repetition for the sake of awe, a repetition that indicates its increase, meaning: it exceeds the limit of description and expression. It is therefore of the type of verbal emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi). This is joined with the particle thumma (then), which, when it conjoins one sentence to another, is characteristically used to express rutbi tarakhi (a gradual distance in rank), meaning the distance in rank within the purpose for which the speech is directed. In this context, that rank is the rank of magnificence and awe, so the "tarakhi" (lapse or distance) in it is the increase.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 82, verse 19:**

﴿On a Day when no soul will have power to do anything for another soul.﴾

This is an explanation of the great but general terror that was conveyed by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is? Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 17–18]. Terror suggests that what the terrified fear will come to pass, so He followed this with an increase in the terror, together with a removal of hope in finding any helper or supporter.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read *yawma* with a *fatha*. It may then be a *badal mutabiq* (a substitute that agrees with its referent, i.e. a substitute in complete correspondence) or an *'atf bayan* (explicative apposition) of *yawmu al-Din*, which is *marfu'* (nominative) by *﴿ma adraka﴾* [al-Infitar: 18]. Its *fatha* is then a *fatha* of indeclinability (*bina'*), because when a noun of time is annexed to a verbal clause whose verb is inflected (*mu'rab*), it is permissible for the noun of time to be indeclinable on the *fatha*, or to be inflected according to the governing words.

It is also permissible for it to be a *badal mutabiq* of *yawma al-Din*, which is in the accusative as a adverb of time in His saying: ﴿They will burn therein on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Infitar: 15]. The clarification of the vagueness in His saying ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 17] is not lost, because *yawmu al-Din* (in the nominative), mentioned second, is the very same as *yawma al-Din* (in the accusative), mentioned first. So when the first mention is clarified, the second mention is clarified too, since both refer to one and the same day.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it *marfu'a* (in the nominative), so it must be a *badal* or a *bayan* of *yawmu al-Din* in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 17].

The meaning of ﴿no soul will have power to do anything for another soul﴾ is: no soul will be able to do anything for the sake of another soul, that is, for its benefit. This is because the proper usage of the *lam* of purpose (*lam al-ta'lil*) is to introduce the one who benefits from an action, unlike *'ala*, which introduces the one who is harmed, as in His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it earned﴾ [al-Baqara: 286].

This was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿I cannot avail you anything against God﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 4], in surah al-Mumtahana.

The generality of *nafs* (soul) in both its occurrences, within a context of negation, requires the generality of the ruling for every soul.

*Shay'an* (anything) is a noun that denotes the category of what exists. It is extremely vague, and its vagueness is resolved by what accompanies it in speech, such as a specification (*tamyiz*), a qualifier (*sifa*), or the like, or by the context. Here it is clarified by what is indicated by the verb ﴿cannot own﴾ and by the *lam* of cause. That is: anything that would avail or benefit it, as in His saying: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God﴾ [Yusuf: 67], in surah Yusuf. Thus *shay'an* is in the accusative as the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*) of the verb ﴿cannot own﴾. That is: there will be nothing within their power that benefits another soul.

This conveys the despair of the polytheists of ever being benefited by their idols on that day, as He said: ﴿And we do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners among you﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

﴿And the command on that Day belongs to God﴾

The sentence ﴿And the command on that Day belongs to God﴾ is a *tadhyil* (a concluding sentence that generalises the preceding statement). The definite article in *al-amr* (the command) is for generalisation (*al-istighraq*). Here *al-amr* means authority and permission, and it is the singular of *al-awamir* (commands). That is: none commands except God. It is also possible that *al-amr* is synonymous with *al-shay'* (thing), and the change of expression is for variety.

The definite article in both interpretations is the definite article of the category, used to mean generalisation, so it covers all affairs. With this generality the sentence serves as a concluding statement.

The *lam* of exclusivity (*lam al-ikhtisas*), together with the generality of *al-amr*, conveys that on that day there is no command except that of God alone, and no action proceeds from anyone else. There is no explicit exclusive formula in this construction, but it reverts to the meaning of exclusivity, in the manner discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿Praise be to God﴾.

In this conclusion there is a *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (return of the end to the beginning), because the surah began with a report about some of the conditions of the Day of Recompense, and it ends with some of its conditions.

Surah al-Mutaffifin

This surah is named in the books of Sunnah and in some works of tafsir (exegesis) as *Surat Wayl lil-Mutaffifin* (the Surah of "Woe to the defrauders"). Al-Bukhari included it under the Book of Tafsir in his Sahih, and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami'.

It is named in many books of tafsir and in the mushafs as *Surat al-Mutaffifin*, for brevity.

In al-Itqan he did not mention it among the surahs that have more than one name, and he named it *Surat al-Mutaffifin*. This requires examination.

There is disagreement over whether it is Meccan, Medinan, or partly Meccan and partly Medinan. From Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Muqatil (in one report from him) it is Meccan. From Ibn 'Abbas (in the more correct report from him), 'Ikrima, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and Muqatil (in another report from him) it is Medinan. He said: "It is the first surah revealed in Medina." From Ibn 'Abbas (in one report from him) and Qatada: it is Medinan except for its last eight verses, from His saying ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29] to its end.

Al-Kalbi and Jabir ibn Zayd said: it was revealed between Mecca and Medina, so it is Meccan in that sense, because according to the preferred opinion of the scholars of the Qur'an, what counts as Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijra.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: some exegetes argued that it is Meccan because of the mention of legends in it, that is, His saying: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says: "Legends of the ancients"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 13]. What we prefer is that it was revealed before the Hijra, because most of its content is an allusion to those who deny the Resurrection.

Among the subtleties is that it may have been revealed between Mecca and Medina, because defrauding was widespread in both towns. From their disagreement it follows that it is either the last of what was revealed at Mecca or the first of what was revealed at Medina. The view that it was revealed between Mecca and Medina is a good view.

Al-Wahidi mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were among the worst of people in measuring. So God Most High revealed ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1], and after that they measured well."

From al-Qurazi: "There were merchants in Medina who cheated in measuring, and their dealings were like the earnings of gambling, and the sales of touching (*mulamasa*), throwing (*munabadha*), and hand-clasping (*mukhasara*). So God Most High revealed this verse, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to the market and recited it. This was a habit that had spread among them since the time of polytheism, and some of those who had embraced Islam among the people of Medina did not notice what it involved of consuming people's property. So it was intended to awaken them to this, and it was an introduction to correcting the conditions of the Muslims in Medina, together with denouncing the conditions of the polytheists in Mecca and Yathrib, in that they were the ones who had established defrauding."

How fitting is this purpose to the view that it was revealed between Mecca and Medina, in order to purify Medina from corruption in commercial dealings before the Prophet (ﷺ) entered it, so that he would not witness a general wrong in it. For measuring and weighing are never free of time from being used in markets and exchanges.

It is numbered as the eighty-sixth in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after surah al-'Ankabut and before surah al-Baqara.

The number of its verses is thirty-six.

And that this is among the things for which they will be held accountable on the Day of Resurrection.
